question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{4}, & \,1\le x\le 3 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. 
Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=2]$ given that the conditional probability density function ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)$ is shown above.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=2] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x\cdot \frac{x}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{12}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{27}{12}-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{13}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Conditional Expectation From a Conditional PDF
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=2] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x\cdot \frac{x}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{12}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{27}{12}-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{13}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{4}, & \,1\le x\le 3 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=2] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x\cdot \frac{x}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{12}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{27}{12}-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{13}{6}.\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+3y}{12}, & 1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y+1}{4}, & 0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2x+3y}{12})}{(\frac{y+1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{2x+3y}{3y+3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{2x+3\cdot 1}{3\cdot 1+3}=\frac{2x+3}{6}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{2x+3}{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{1}^{2}(2{x}^{2}+3x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}((\frac{16}{3}+6)-(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{2})) \\  & =\frac{55}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of Y are shown above. Find the conditional expected value E[X|Y=1].

5536

Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of X given Y=y is defined by

E[X|Y=y]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|y)dx.

Note that E[X|Y=y] is a function of y.

The conditional density function of X given Y=y can be computed as

fX|Y(x|y)=f(x,y)fY(y)=(2x+3y12)(y+14)=2x+3y3y+3,

where 1≤x≤2,0≤y≤2. Outside this domain, we have fX|Y(x|y)=0.

Now, substituting y=1 into the expression for fX|Y(x|y), we get

fX|Y(x|1)=2x+3⋅13⋅1+3=2x+36.

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[X|Y=1]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|1)dx=∫12x⋅2x+36dx=16∫12(2x2+3x)dx=16[2x33+3x22]12=16((163+6)−(23+32))=5536.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2x+3y}{12})}{(\frac{y+1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{2x+3y}{3y+3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{2x+3\cdot 1}{3\cdot 1+3}=\frac{2x+3}{6}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{2x+3}{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{1}^{2}(2{x}^{2}+3x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}((\frac{16}{3}+6)-(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{2})) \\  & =\frac{55}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{2x+3}{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{1}^{2}(2{x}^{2}+3x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}((\frac{16}{3}+6)-(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{2})) \\  & =\frac{55}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}12xy, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}6{x}^{5}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as  

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{12xy}{6{x}^{5}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{4}},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0<x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|1\,)=2y.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot (2y)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of X are shown above. Find the conditional expected value E[Y|X=1].

a

EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of Y given X=x is defined by

E[Y|X=x]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|x)dy.

Note that E[Y|X=x] is a function of x.

The conditional density function of Y given X=x can be computed as

fY|X(y|x)=f(x,y)fX(x)=12xy6x5=2yx4,

where 0<x≤1,0≤y≤x2. Outside this domain, we have fY|X(y|x)=0.

Now, substituting x=1 into the expression for fY|X(y|x), we get

fY|X(y|1)=2y. Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[Y|X=1]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|1)dy=∫01y⋅(2y)dy=∫01(2y2)dy=[2y33]01=23.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}12xy, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}6{x}^{5}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as  

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{12xy}{6{x}^{5}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{4}},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0<x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|1\,)=2y.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot (2y)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}2-x-y, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}-y, & 0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(2-x-y)}{(\frac{3}{2}-y)} \\  & =\frac{4-2x-2y}{3-2y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{4-2x-2\cdot 1}{3-2\cdot 1}=\frac{4-2x-2}{3-2}=2-2x.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(2-2x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x-2{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating Conditional Expectations Given Joint and Marginal PDFs
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(2-x-y)}{(\frac{3}{2}-y)} \\  & =\frac{4-2x-2y}{3-2y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{4-2x-2\cdot 1}{3-2\cdot 1}=\frac{4-2x-2}{3-2}=2-2x.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(2-2x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x-2{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8

f(x,y)={2−x−y,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1,0,otherwisefY(y)={32−y,0≤y≤1,0,otherwise

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of Y are shown above. Find the conditional expected value E[X|Y=1].

a
13
b
1
c
43
d
23
e
16
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of X given Y=y is defined by

E[X|Y=y]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|y)dx.

Note that E[X|Y=y] is a function of y.

The conditional density function of X given Y=y can be computed as

fX|Y(x|y)=f(x,y)fY(y)=(2−x−y)(32−y)=4−2x−2y3−2y,

where 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1. Outside this domain, we have fX|Y(x|y)=0.

Now, substituting y=1 into the expression for fX|Y(x|y), we get

fX|Y(x|1)=4−2x−2⋅13−2⋅1=4−2x−23−2=2−2x.

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[X|Y=1]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|1)dx=∫01x(2−2x)dx=∫01(2x−2x2)dx=[x2−2x33]01=(1−23)−0=13.

solution.reasoning: Since f_Y(1)=1/2, the conditional density is f_{X|Y}(x|1)=2(1-x) for 0≤x≤1. Thus E[X|Y=1]=\int_0^1 2x(1-x)\,dx=[x^2-2x^3/3]_0^1=\frac{1}{3}, option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different distribution.

Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3x+{y}^{2}}{8})}{(\frac{3x+1}{8})} \\  & =\frac{3(x+{y}^{2})}{3x+1},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{3\cdot 1+1}=\frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{4}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{4}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4})-0] \\  & =\frac{9}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3(x+{y}^{2})}{8}, & 0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3x+1}{8}, & 0\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3x+{y}^{2}}{8})}{(\frac{3x+1}{8})} \\  & =\frac{3(x+{y}^{2})}{3x+1},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{3\cdot 1+1}=\frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{4}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{4}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4})-0] \\  & =\frac{9}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}8xy, & 0<x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le x, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}, & 0<x\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{8xy}{4{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0<x\le 1,\,0<y\le x.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$    

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|1\,)=2y.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot (2y)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating Conditional Expectations Given Joint and Marginal PDFs
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{8xy}{4{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0<x\le 1,\,0<y\le x.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$    

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|1\,)=2y.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot (2y)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of X are shown above. Find the conditional expected value E[Y|X=1].

a
23
b
13
c
45
d
25
e
 32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of Y given X=x is defined by

E[Y|X=x]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|x)dy.

Note that E[Y|X=x] is a function of x.

The conditional density function of Y given X=x can be computed as

fY|X(y|x)=f(x,y)fX(x)=8xy4x3=2yx2,

where 0<x≤1,0<y≤x. Outside this domain, we have fY|X(y|x)=0.

Now, substituting x=1 into the expression for fY|X(y|x), we get

fY|X(y|1)=2y. Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[Y|X=1]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|1)dy=∫01y⋅(2y)dy=∫01(2y2)dy=[2y33]01=23.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}, & 0\le y\le 4,\,0<x<\frac{1}{2} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}24{x}^{2}, & 0<x<\frac{1}{2} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ for $0<x<\frac{1}{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}}{24{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le y\le 4,\,0<x<\frac{1}{2}.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}y\cdot \,\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{16}{2}-0] \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Conditional Expectation as a Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}}{24{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le y\le 4,\,0<x<\frac{1}{2}.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}y\cdot \,\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{16}{2}-0] \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{6(x+y)}{5}, & x\le y\le 2x,\,0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}, & 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ for $0<x<1.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6(x+y)}{5})}{3{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+y)}{5{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x\le y\le 2x,\,0<x<1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{x}^{2x}y\cdot \,\frac{2(x+y)}{5{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5{x}^{2}}{\int }_{x}^{2x}(xy+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5{x}^{2}}{[\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{x}^{2x} \\  & =\frac{2}{5{x}^{2}}[(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{8{x}^{3}}{3})-(\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})] \\  & =\frac{2}{5{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{23{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cancel{{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{23x\cdot \cancel{({x}^{2})}}{3} \\  & =\frac{23x}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of X are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value E[Y|X=x] for 0<x<1.

b

c
23x15

Recall that the conditional expected value of Y given X=x is defined by

E[Y|X=x]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|x)dy.

fY|X(y|x)=f(x,y)fX(x)=(6(x+y)5)3x2=2(x+y)5x2,

$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x+2y)}{3}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1+4y}{3}, & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ for $0\le y\le 1.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2(x+2y)}{3})}{(\frac{1+4y}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+2yx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+y{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}\cdot [\frac{1}{3}+y-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}\cdot \frac{1+3y}{3} \\  & =\frac{2(1+3y)}{3(1+4y)}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Conditional Expectation as a Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2(x+2y)}{3})}{(\frac{1+4y}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+2yx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+y{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}\cdot [\frac{1}{3}+y-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}\cdot \frac{1+3y}{3} \\  & =\frac{2(1+3y)}{3(1+4y)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x+2y)}{3}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1+4y}{3}, & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ for $0\le y\le 1.$

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of Y are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value E[X|Y=y] for 0≤y≤1.

a
(1+4y)(1+3y)
b
(1+3y)(1+4y)
c
2(1+3y)3(1+4y)
d
(1+3y)3(1+4y)
e
(y+3)3(y+4)

EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of X given Y=y is defined by

E[X|Y=y]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|y)dx.

Note that E[X|Y=y] is a function of y.

The conditional density function of X given X=x can be computed as

fX|Y(x|y)=f(x,y)fY(y)=(2(x+2y)3)(1+4y3)=2(x+2y)1+4y,

where 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1. Outside this domain, we have fY|X(y|x)=0.

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[X|Y=y]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|y)dx=∫01x⋅2(x+2y)1+4ydx=21+4y∫01(x2+2yx)dx=21+4y[x33+yx2]01=21+4y⋅[13+y−0]=21+4y⋅1+3y3=2(1+3y)3(1+4y).
question.knowledge_point: Conditional Expectation as a Function

solution.reasoning: The conditional density is f_{X|Y}(x|y)=2(x+2y)/(1+4y) for 0≤x≤1. Thus E[X|Y=y]=\frac{2}{1+4y}\int_0^1(x^2+2yx)\,dx=\frac{2}{1+4y}(\frac{1}{3}+y)=\frac{2(1+3y)}{3(1+4y)}, option c. feedback.name: Question 14
feedback.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x+2y)}{3}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1+4y}{3}, & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ for $0\le y\le 1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2(x+2y)}{3})}{(\frac{1+4y}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+2yx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+y{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}\cdot [\frac{1}{3}+y-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}\cdot \frac{1+3y}{3} \\  & =\frac{2(1+3y)}{3(1+4y)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{5}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0<y<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{6y+2}{5}, & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ for $0<y<1.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{5})}{(\frac{6y+2}{5})} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}+xy)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}y}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{y}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}\cdot \frac{1+2y}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{2(3y+1)}\cdot \frac{(1+2y)}{4} \\  & =\frac{3(1+2y)}{4(3y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Conditional Expectation as a Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{5})}{(\frac{6y+2}{5})} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}+xy)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}y}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{y}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}\cdot \frac{1+2y}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{2(3y+1)}\cdot \frac{(1+2y)}{4} \\  & =\frac{3(1+2y)}{4(3y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of Y are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value E[X|Y=y] for 0<y<1.

a
3y24(y+3)
b
(1+2y)(3y+1)
c
2y2(3y+1)
d
(1+2y)4(3y+1)
e
3(1+2y)4(3y+1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of X given Y=y is defined by

E[X|Y=y]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|y)dx.

Note that E[X|Y=y] is a function of y.

The conditional density function of X given X=x can be computed as

fX|Y(x|y)=f(x,y)fY(y)=(6x2+6y5)(6y+25)=6x2+6y6y+2,

where 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1. Outside this domain, we have fY|X(y|x)=0.

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[X|Y=y]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|y)dx=∫01x⋅6x2+6y6y+2dx=66y+2∫01(x3+xy)dx=66y+2[x44+x2y2]01=66y+2[14+y2−0]=66y+2⋅1+2y4=62(3y+1)⋅(1+2y)4=3(1+2y)4(3y+1).

solution.reasoning: The conditional density is f_{X|Y}(x|y)=3(x^2+y)/(3y+1) for 0≤x≤1. Therefore E[X|Y=y]=\frac{3}{3y+1}\int_0^1(x^3+yx)\,dx=\frac{3}{3y+1}(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{y}{2})=\frac{3(1+2y)}{4(3y+1)}, option e. $$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ for $0<y<1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{5})}{(\frac{6y+2}{5})} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}+xy)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}y}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{y}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}\cdot \frac{1+2y}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{2(3y+1)}\cdot \frac{(1+2y)}{4} \\  & =\frac{3(1+2y)}{4(3y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

f(x,y)={6x2+6y5,0≤x≤1,0<y<10,otherwisefY(y)={6y+25,0≤y≤10,otherwise

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of Y are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value E[X|Y=y] for 0<y<1.

a
3y24(y+3)
b
(1+2y)(3y+1)
c
2y2(3y+1)
d
(1+2y)4(3y+1)
e
3(1+2y)4(3y+1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of X given Y=y is defined by

E[X|Y=y]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|y)dx.

Note that E[X|Y=y] is a function of y.

The conditional density function of X given X=x can be computed as

fX|Y(x|y)=f(x,y)fY(y)=(6x2+6y5)(6y+25)=6x2+6y6y+2,

where 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1. Outside this domain, we have fY|X(y|x)=0.

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[X|Y=y]=∫−∞∞xfX|Y(x|y)dx=∫01x⋅6x2+6y6y+2dx=66y+2∫01(x3+xy)dx=66y+2[x44+x2y2]01=66y+2[14+y2−0]=66y+2⋅1+2y4=62(3y+1)⋅(1+2y)4=3(1+2y)4(3y+1).

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14202834/assets/42e163dd119aaea37d2a373310b408a409023400a6f84ff520c464c6acb153b9.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0.3)$ | $0.3$ | $(0.3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |

Additionally, the function has an inflection point at $x≈-0.3.$ So ${f}^{″}(-0.3)≈0$ and the tangent to the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis.

We don't know the exact value of ${f}^{′}(-0.3)$ but from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that at $x≈-0.3,$ the slope is positive.

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14202834/assets/b1b048d1b6c430f023c0419d7c8442740b76b5d7e646f32fc870be9225649b70.png)

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14202834/assets/174178e1d4c527bb81ea3ba726e5ef753b40dd85b452d65faf05590e7a387a32.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function is piecewise-linear, we get a constant derivative over each linear part.
Notice the following:

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

- When $f(x)$ is constant, we get ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $\text{const.}$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $\text{undef.}$ | $0$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. 

Additionally, we have a change of the slope of the tangent line (from negative to $0$) when we pass through $x=4$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=4$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14202834/assets/877fcf017ab91010648de9a375e535ec7697841c8e317196c5759df6aca32e19.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Since the function is piecewise-linear, we get a constant derivative over each linear part.
Notice the following:

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $\text{undef.}$ | $-$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. 

Additionally, we have a change of the slope of the tangent line (from positive to negative)  when we pass through $x=0$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=0$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1,$ and determine which of the following statements is true.
questions.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ x+3y+5=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get

$$
H(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-6y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-6x.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y=0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-6x=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
3{x}^{2}-6y=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})}^{2}-6x & =0 \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{4}-8x & =0 \\ x({x}^{3}-8) & =0 \\ x & =0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
x=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}=0,\,\,x=2\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}=2.
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=6x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=-6 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=-6\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=6y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6x & -6 \\ -6 & 6y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=0\cdot 0-(-6)^{2}=-36<0.
$$

Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2,2)=[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(2,2),$ we get

$$
H(2,2)=det({f}^{″}(2,2))=12\cdot 12-(-6)^{2}=108>0.
$$

Finally, since $H(2,2)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,2)=({f}^{″}(2,2))_{11}=12>0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(2,2).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(2,2).$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2(xy-3)\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xy-3=0 \\ {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
xy-3=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{x}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9{(\frac{3}{x})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{{x}^{4}-81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-81 & =0 \\ x & =-3,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{3}{x},$ we obtain

$$
x=-3\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{-3}=-1,\,\,x=3\,\,\,\,\,\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{3}=1.
$$

Hence, $(-3,-1)$ and $(3,1)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-6)=2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-6)=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=-18y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -18y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,1)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 6 & -18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(3,1),$ we get

$$
H(3,1)=det({f}^{″}(3,1))=2\cdot (-18)-{6}^{2}=-72<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(3,1)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(-3,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-3,-1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -6 \\ -6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-3,-1),$ we get

$$
H(-3,-1)=det({f}^{″}(-3,-1))=(-2)\cdot 18-(-6)^{2}=-72<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(-3,-1)$ is a saddle point.

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(3,1)$ and $(-3,-1).$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the first derivative

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],
$$

and has a stationary point at $(3,-3).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(3,-3)>0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)<0$

III. The point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum of $f$
questions.worked_solution:
The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x+2y-6,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y-6)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+2y)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,-3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,-3)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(3,-3),$ we get

$$
H(3,-3)=det({f}^{″}(3,-3))=4\cdot 2-{2}^{2}=4>0.
$$

- Statement II is false. We have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)=({f}^{″}(3,-3))_{11}=4>0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(3,-3)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)>0,$ the point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the first derivative

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],
$$

and has a stationary point at $(-1,1).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(-1,1)<0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0$

III. The point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum of $f$
questions.worked_solution:
The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})=\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & -\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1,1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(-1,1),$ we get

$$
H(-1,1)=det({f}^{″}(-1,1))=(-2)^{2}-(-1)^{2}=3>0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)=({f}^{″}(-1,1))_{11}=-2<0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(-1,1)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0,$ the point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ x+3y+5=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get

$$
H(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$

Question 2
?

Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function f(x,y) given that f′(x,y)=[3x2−6y3y2−6x].

a
f(x,y) has a local minimum at (0,0) and a saddle point at (−2,−2)
b
f(x,y) has a local minimum at (0,0) and a local maximum at (−2,−2)
c
f(x,y) has a saddle point at (0,0) and a local maximum at (2,2)
d
f(x,y) has a saddle point at (0,0) and a local minimum at (2,2)
e
f(x,y) has saddle points at (0,0) and (2,2)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The local extrema of f occur at its critical points. A point a in the domain of f is a critical point of f if f′(a)=0T (for stationary points) or f′(a) doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if a∈R2 is a stationary point of f(x,y) with Hessian determinant H(a), we have the following:

  • If H(a)>0, then:

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)<0, then f has a local maximum at a

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)>0, then f has a local minimum at a

  • If H(a)<0, then f has a saddle point at a

  • If H(a)=0, then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since f′(x,y)=[3x2−6y3y2−6x], we must have

∂f∂x=3x2−6y,∂f∂y=3y2−6x.

The first derivative exists for any (x,y) in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting f′(x,y)=0T, we obtain the following system:

{3x2−6y=03y2−6x=0.

Solving the first equation for y, we get

3x2−6y=0⟹y=12x2.

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

3(12x2)2−6x=014x4−2x=0x4−8x=0x(x3−8)=0x=0,2.

Back-substituting these values into y=12x2, we obtain

x=0⟹y=12(0)2=0,x=2⟹y=12(2)2=2.

Hence, (0,0) and (2,2) are stationary points of f(x,y).

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(3x2−6y)=6x∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(3y2−6x)=−6∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(3x2−6y)=−6∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(3y2−6x)=6y

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]=[6x−6−66y].

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

  • Evaluating the second derivative at (0,0), we obtain f″(0,0)=[0−6−60]. Computing the determinant H(0,0), we get H(0,0)=det(f″(0,0))=0⋅0−(−6)2=−36<0. Therefore, f(0,0) is a saddle point.

  • Evaluating the second derivative at (2,2), we obtain f″(2,2)=[12−6−612]. Computing the determinant H(2,2), we get H(2,2)=det(f″(2,2))=12⋅12−(−6)2=108>0. Finally, since H(2,2)>0 and ∂2f∂x2(2,2)=(f″(2,2))11=12>0, the function f has a local minimum at (2,2).

In conclusion, f(x,y) has a saddle point at (0,0) and a local minimum at (2,2).

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2(xy-3)\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xy-3=0 \\ {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
xy-3=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{x}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9{(\frac{3}{x})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{{x}^{4}-81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-81 & =0 \\ x & =-3,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{3}{x},$ we obtain

$$
x=-3\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{-3}=-1,\,\,x=3\,\,\,\,\,\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{3}=1.
$$

Hence, $(-3,-1)$ and $(3,1)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-6)=2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-6)=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=-18y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -18y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,1)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 6 & -18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(3,1),$ we get

$$
H(3,1)=det({f}^{″}(3,1))=2\cdot (-18)-{6}^{2}=-72<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(3,1)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(-3,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-3,-1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -6 \\ -6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-3,-1),$ we get

$$
H(-3,-1)=det({f}^{″}(-3,-1))=(-2)\cdot 18-(-6)^{2}=-72<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(-3,-1)$ is a saddle point.

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(3,1)$ and $(-3,-1).$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function f(x,y) given that f′(x,y)=[2(xy−3)x2−9y2].

a
f(x,y) has a local minimum at (−3,1) and a saddle point at (−3,1)
b
f(x,y) has a local maximum at (−3,1) and a local minimum (−3,1)
c
f(x,y) has saddle points at (3,1) and (−3,−1)
d
f(x,y) has a saddle point at (3,1) and a local maximum (−3,−1)
e
f(x,y) has a local minimum at (3,1) and a local maximum (−3,−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The local extrema of f occur at its critical points. A point a in the domain of f is a critical point of f if f′(a)=0T (for stationary points) or f′(a) doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if a∈R2 is a stationary point of f(x,y) with Hessian determinant H(a), we have the following:

  • If H(a)>0, then:

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)<0, then f has a local maximum at a

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)>0, then f has a local minimum at a

  • If H(a)<0, then f has a saddle point at a

  • If H(a)=0, then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since f′(x,y)=[2(xy−3)x2−9y2], we must have

∂f∂x=2(xy−3)∂f∂y=x2−9y2.

The first derivative exists for any (x,y) in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting f′(x,y)=0T, we obtain the following system:

{xy−3=0x2−9y2=0 Solving the first equation for y, we get xy−3=0⟹y=3x.

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

x2−9(3x)2=0x2−81x2=0x4−81x2=0x2−81=0x=−3,3.

Back-substituting these values into y=3x, we obtain

x=−3⟹y=3−3=−1,x=3⟹y=33=1.

Hence, (−3,−1) and (3,1) are stationary points of f(x,y).

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2xy−6)=2y∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(x2−9y2)=2x∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2xy−6)=2x∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(x2−9y2)=−18y

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂x∂y]=[2y2x2x−18y].

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

  • Evaluating the second derivative at (3,1), we obtain f″(3,1)=[266−18]. Computing the determinant H(3,1), we get H(3,1)=det(f″(3,1))=2⋅(−18)−62=−72<0, Therefore, f(3,1) is a saddle point.

  • Evaluating the second derivative at (−3,−1), we obtain f″(−3,−1)=[−2−6−618]. Computing the determinant H(−3,−1), we get H(−3,−1)=det(f″(−3,−1))=(−2)⋅18−(−6)2=−72<0, Therefore, f(−3,−1) is a saddle point.

In conclusion, f(x,y) has saddle points at (3,1) and (−3,−1).

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x+2y-6,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y-6)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+2y)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,-3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,-3)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(3,-3),$ we get

$$
H(3,-3)=det({f}^{″}(3,-3))=4\cdot 2-{2}^{2}=4>0.
$$

- Statement II is false. We have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)=({f}^{″}(3,-3))_{11}=4>0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(3,-3)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)>0,$ the point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})=\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & -\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1,1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(-1,1),$ we get

$$
H(-1,1)=det({f}^{″}(-1,1))=(-2)^{2}-(-1)^{2}=3>0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)=({f}^{″}(-1,1))_{11}=-2<0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(-1,1)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0,$ the point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

The function f(x,y) has the first derivative f′(x,y)=[1−yx21x+1y2], and has a stationary point at (−1,1). If H denotes the Hessian determinant of f, which of the following statements are true?

  1. H(−1,1)<0
  2. ∂2f∂x2(−1,1)<0
  3. The point (−1,1) is a local maximum of f
a
I and II only
b
I only
c
II only
d
II and III only
e
III only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The second partial derivative test states that if a∈R2 is a stationary point of f(x,y) with Hessian determinant H(a), we have the following:

  • If H(a)>0, then:

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)<0, then f has a local maximum at a

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)>0, then f has a local minimum at a

  • If H(a)<0, then f has a saddle point at a

  • If H(a)=0, then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since f′(x,y)=[1−yx21x+1y2], we must have

∂f∂x=1−yx2,∂f∂y=1x+1y2.

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(1−yx2)=2yx3∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(1x+1y2)=−2y3∂2f∂x∂y=∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂x(1x+1y2)=−1x2

So, the second derivative is f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]=[2yx3−1x2−1x2−2y3].

Evaluating the second derivative at (−1,1), we obtain f″(−1,1)=[−2−1−1−2].

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of f″(−1,1), we get H(−1,1)=det(f″(−1,1))=(−2)2−(−1)2=3>0.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, we have ∂2f∂x2(−1,1)=(f″(−1,1))11=−2<0.

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, since H(−1,1)>0 and ∂2f∂x2(−1,1)<0, the point (−1,1) is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1,$ and determine which of the following statements is true.
question.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ x+3y+5=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get

$$
H(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function f(x,y)=x2+2xy+3y2+2x+10y+1, and determine which of the following statements is true.

a
f(x,y) has a local maximum at (−3,2)
b
f(x,y) has a local maximum at (1,−2)
c
f(x,y) has a local minimum at (−3,2)
d
f(x,y) has a local minimum at (1,−2)
e
f(x,y) has a saddle point at (1,−2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The local extrema of f occur at its critical points. A point a in the domain of f is a critical point of f if f′(a)=0T (for stationary points) or f′(a) doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if a∈R2 is a stationary point of f(x,y) with Hessian determinant H(a), we have the following:

  • If H(a)>0, then:

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)<0, then f has a local maximum at a

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)>0, then f has a local minimum at a

  • If H(a)<0, then f has a saddle point at a

  • If H(a)=0, then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(x2+2xy+3y2+2x+10y+1)∂∂y(x2+2xy+3y2+2x+10y+1)]=[2(x+y+1)2(x+3y+5)]

The first derivative exists for any (x,y) in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting f′(x,y)=0T, we obtain the following system:

{x+y+1=0x+3y+5=0.

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get 2y+4=0⟹y=−2.

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain x+(−2)+1=0⟹x=1. Hence, (1,−2) is a stationary point of f(x,y).

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2(x+y+1))=2∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2(x+3y+5))=2∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2(x+y+1))=2∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2(x+3y+5))=6

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]=[2226].

Evaluating the second derivative at (1,−2), we obtain

f″(1,−2)=[2226].

Computing the determinant H(1,−2), we get H(1,−2)=det(f″(1,−2))=2⋅6−22=8>0.

Finally, notice that ∂2f∂x2(1,−2)=(f″(1,−2))11=2>0.

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that f(x,y) has a local minimum at (1,−2).

last_observation.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ x+3y+5=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$

f(x,y) has a local maximum at (−3,2)
b
f(x,y) has a local maximum at (1,−2)
c
f(x,y) has a local minimum at (−3,2)

  • If H(a)>0, then:

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)<0, then f has a local maximum at a

    • if ∂2f∂x2(a)>0, then f has a local minimum at a

  • If H(a)<0, then f has a saddle point at a

  • If H(a)=0, then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(x2+2xy+3y2+2x+10y+1)∂∂y(x2+2xy+3y2+2x+10y+1)]=[2(x+y+1)2(x+3y+5)]

The first derivative exists for any (x,y) in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting f′(x,y)=0T, we obtain the following system:

{x+y+1=0x+3y+5=0.

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get 2y+4=0⟹y=−2.

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain x+(−2)+1=0⟹x=1. Hence, (1,−2) is a stationary point of f(x,y).

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2(x+y+1))=2∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2(x+3y+5))=2∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2(x+y+1))=2∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2(x+3y+5))=6

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]=[2226].

Evaluating the second derivative at (1,−2), we obtain

f″(1,−2)=[2226].

Computing the determinant H(1,−2), we get H(1,−2)=det(f″(1,−2))=2⋅6−22=8>0.

Finally, notice that ∂2f∂x2(1,−2)=(f″(1,−2))11=2>0.

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that f(x,y) has a local minimum at (1,−2).

  • If H(a)<0, then f has a saddle point at a
